summary:
ASTRA HEALTH is a decision support system built to monitor astronaut health during long-duration space missions. In space, reaching a physician right away is not always possible, and health problems often develop slowly and go unnoticed. The goal of the project is to catch these quiet changes early and alert both the astronaut and the ground control team in time.

The system brings together the astronaut’s measurements such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, oxygen level and eye pressure; daily self-reports such as sleep, mood, stress and loneliness; and the results of attention and reaction tests, all in a single panel. It compares each astronaut not against a general average but against their own history. This way, a change that is unusual for that person becomes visible before it reaches dangerous levels.

When a deviation is found, the system explains it in plain language and offers suitable recommendations drawn from knowledge cards based on NASA sources. For example, it gives sleep routine advice to an astronaut whose sleep is deteriorating, and suggests crew activities to one whose loneliness is rising. In serious cases it asks for the flight physician to be notified and sends an alert to the ground control team.

ASTRA HEALTH does not diagnose; it leaves the decision to people. Its job is to help protect crew health and mission safety by getting the right information to the right person at the right time.
details:
ASTRA HEALTH is a decision support system that monitors astronaut health during long-duration space missions and warns both the crew member and ground control when something starts to go wrong.

What it does and how it works

The system collects three kinds of data in one place: physiological measurements (heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, blood oxygen, eye pressure, radiation dose and cabin CO2), daily self-reports (mood, stress, sleep, loneliness, crew relations and symptoms), and short cognitive tests that measure reaction time and attention.

Each day's values are compared against two references. The first is the astronaut's own history: the system builds a personal baseline from that person's previous days and flags anything that departs from it. The second is a set of fixed safety limits, such as a minimum blood oxygen level. When a deviation is found, the system selects relevant entries from a library of 76 knowledge cards drawn from NASA technical reports and standards, and a locally running language model writes a short, plain-language explanation of what changed. Recommendations are taken directly from the approved cards. Serious findings are escalated to the flight physician, and ground control receives an alert in real time.

Benefits

Health problems in space often develop slowly, and a value can be unusual for one person while still sitting inside a general "normal" range. Comparing each astronaut to their own baseline makes these changes visible earlier. Because physical, psychological and cognitive data are viewed together, the system can connect signals that would be missed in isolation, for example poor sleep alongside slower reaction times. Every explanation cites its source, so the crew and physicians can check where the advice comes from.

Intended impact

On missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays mean a crew cannot always rely on immediate medical guidance from Earth. ASTRA HEALTH is meant to give astronauts more medical autonomy by getting the right information to the right person at the right time, while keeping ground control informed. The same approach could support people in other isolated settings, such as polar stations, submarines or remote clinics.

Tools and technologies

The backend is written in Python with FastAPI, SQLAlchemy and Alembic, on a Microsoft SQL Server 2022 database. The interface is built with React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS, with Recharts for charts and three.js for an interactive 3D body model. The language model is Qwen3 14B, run locally through Ollama. Docker Compose runs the whole stack, and pytest plus an isolated end-to-end test environment verify it. Demonstration data is synthetic: a 74-day mission scenario with two astronauts whose conditions differ.

How it is creative

The key design choice is that the AI explains but never decides. Risk level, card selection and recommendations are produced by transparent, deterministic rules; the language model only writes the summary. If the model is unavailable, the same decision is still produced and no alert is lost. The model runs on the local machine, so sensitive health data never leaves the spacecraft and the system does not depend on a connection to Earth. The 3D body view lets an astronaut see at a glance which part of the body a finding relates to. To show that the output is truly personal, our demo includes two crew members: one with a slow decline over two weeks, and one with a sudden cardio-respiratory event, each receiving different findings and different guidance from the same system.

Factors the team considered

Safety came first: the system does not diagnose, it never invents numbers, and when data is insufficient it says so instead of reporting "normal". We considered privacy, giving the astronaut and ground control separate roles and limiting database access to the minimum required. We considered trust, tying every recommendation to a cited NASA source. We considered reliability, making sure alerts do not depend on the AI model being available. Finally, we were honest about limits: thresholds and data are for demonstration and are not clinical reference values, and final decisions always remain with people.
